definitions.meaning: to witness a document is to vouch for it with a signature
the place where international cricket is watched

explanation.walkthrough: A Test is an international cricket match, so the second definition splits the answer as AT TEST.
explanation.definitionFit: To witness is to bear formal testimony, and a spectator watching cricket is located at a Test match.

parts.note: tan is a light brown colour
going as in fading away or dying

explanation.surface: A colour that fades under the disco lights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the dance-floor' defines a verb form: doing a Latin ballroom dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Performing the Argentine ballroom dance is what someone is doing out on the dance-floor.

clue.text: Lacking bite, Sir Anthony and Sir Henry

parts.note: Sir Anthony Eden was a British prime minister
Sir Henry Tate was the sugar magnate who founded the Tate Gallery

explanation.surface: Two knights described as toothless.
explanation.walkthrough: Eden was British prime minister 1955-57; Tate was the sugar refiner behind London's Tate Gallery. 'Lacking bite' is literal: without teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals such as sloths and anteaters have few or no teeth, so they lack bite.

clue.text: In a way, three and four, say, make 17

indicators.note: in a way, meaning in an altered fashion, so the letters of three are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written for the rearrangement

indicators.note: say signals a word that is spoken, giving a sound-alike spelling

parts.note: the number four is spoken aloud

explanation.surface: Arithmetic of a sort: three and four add up to a number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a way' rearranges THREE into THERE; 'say' gives FORE for the sound of 'four'. '17' points to the answer to 17 across, which means the same.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer to 17 across is Latin for consequently, the same logical connective.

clue.text: A peg, a dram, and a beer not quite what such a one wants

definitions.text: A peg, a dram, and a beer not quite what such a one wants

parts.note: a golf tee is a small peg the ball sits on
a tot is a small measure of spirits, like a dram

indicators.note: not quite the whole word, so the beer loses its final letter

parts.note: ale is a kind of beer

explanation.surface: A list of drinks and a golf peg, none of which a certain abstainer would want.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite' clips ALE to AL. The whole clue also defines: a teetotaller wants nothing of the drinks listed, so the pieces are 'not quite what such a one wants'.
explanation.definitionFit: A total abstainer from alcohol refuses tots and beers, the very items listed.

clue.text: Play in which swirling dust ruins action

indicators.note: swirling dust is blown about, so the letters of dust, ruins and action are mixed together

explanation.surface: A stage drama where whirling dust spoils the action.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swirling' rearranges DUST RUINS ACTION, all fifteen letters, into the title of Shakespeare's bloodiest tragedy.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's early revenge tragedy is a stage play.

parts.note: a vat is a large tank for liquid
the dropped h of a Cockney 'arsh suggests 'ard, hard said the same way

explanation.surface: Cockney complaint: finding the tax on a mug harsh.
explanation.walkthrough: VAT is the British sales tax in the surface but a tank in the wordplay. The question mark flags the Cockney dropped h: 'arsh for harsh suggests 'ard for hard.
explanation.definitionFit: A large drinking mug, usually for beer, often pewter with a handle.

clue.text: In which a team's backed to win

definitions.text: In which a team's backed to win

parts.words: In which a team's backed to win
parts.note: a contest where each team heaves backwards on a rope, so moving back is how you win

explanation.walkthrough: 'backed' suggests betting, but the team literally pulls backwards on a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Two teams pull opposite ends of a rope, winning by dragging rivals back.

clue.text: See that unending city, : you libertine ?

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or see

indicators.note: unending means the word that loses its final letter

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro, the Brazilian city

explanation.surface: Someone hails a womaniser seen around a city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unending' drops the last letter of 'that' to give THA.
explanation.definitionFit: The seducer in Rowe's play The Fair Penitent gave his name to any rakish womaniser.

definitions.note: blue here means smutty or risqué, an adjective

parts.note: a cricketer who is batting is said to be in
becoming as an adjective means seemly or proper

explanation.surface: A cricketer's innings is turning sad or gloomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming' looks like a verb of change but is the adjective meaning seemly; 'blue' means obscene, not sad.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue jokes or films are lewd, offending against propriety.

definitions.meaning: the title Sir conferred by the monarch is an honour
a chessman shaped like a horse's head is one of the pieces

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is a chess piece; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A dubbing by the sovereign is an honour, and the horse-headed chessman is a playing piece.

definitions.meaning: a keep is the strongest tower of a castle, a stronghold
the Flying ... was a US bomber aircraft of the Second World War

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue: 'bomber ... force airborne' reads as one sentence about the RAF.
explanation.definitionFit: A castle keep is a stronghold, and the B-17 bomber bore that word in its name.

clue.text: … force airborne, if worried by a binder

parts.note: the RAF is Britain's Royal Air Force

indicators.note: worried as in shaken about, so the two letters of if are jumbled

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: an air force bomber troubled by someone who binds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worried' turns IF into FI; 'by' places it beside the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Palm-fibre strands are used to tie plants and parcels, so the material serves as a binder.

indicators.note: out in the sense of disordered, so the letters of counted plus R are rearranged

explanation.surface: A boxer counted out is soundly beaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges COUNTED with R (right) into the answer; the surface's boxing count-out makes 'counted ... out' look like a phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: To be thrashed or defeated decisively is to be soundly beaten.

clue.text: A pretext I explode and destroy

indicators.note: explode means blow apart, so the letters of a pretext I are scattered and reassembled

explanation.surface: Someone vows to blow apart and demolish a flimsy excuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'explode' rearranges A PRETEXT I.
explanation.definitionFit: To root out completely is to destroy, from the Latin for pulling up by the stem.

definitions.note: a bogey is a frightening goblin or monster

indicators.note: round as in turned about, so the two letters of go are swapped

parts.note: re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: Golf talk: going round with a bogey on the card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bogey' looks like the golf score, which suits 'Go round', but here it is the bogeyman. The ellipsis carries this answer into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A bogey is a frightening monster, like the man-eating giant of fairy tales.

parts.note: on means placed upon or applied to
CE is the Church of England
over means finished or completed

explanation.surface: A survey report on a church that is now finished.
explanation.walkthrough: CE stands for the Church of England.
explanation.definitionFit: A quick inspection or look-through is a cursory survey.

indicators.note: enter means go inside, so the academy's letters go into the word for festival

parts.note: a revel is a festive celebration
the RSA is the Royal Scottish Academy, a body of artists

explanation.surface: Artists entering a festival look for sponsorship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Artistic lot' is the Royal Scottish Academy. 'backing' looks like support or sponsorship but means going backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A turn to the opposite direction or a backward move is a reversal.

indicators.note: returning means the carried-over word is read backwards

parts.note: the dots carry over the answer to the previous clue, 15 across

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links back to 15 across: its answer, turned round by 'returning', gives this one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin word for therefore is used in English to mean consequently.

indicators.note: are upset means knocked over and disordered, so the letters of seedings are rearranged

explanation.surface: Tennis players feel nervous when the tournament seedings are overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'are upset' rearranges SEEDINGS; the tennis surface makes 'upset' look like a shock defeat.
explanation.definitionFit: Nervy tension or jumpiness is a state of anxiety.

clue.text: Thousands get one as a ring

definitions.text: Thousands get one as a ring

indicators.note: as a ring means encircling, so get one surrounds the letters for thousands

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so MS is thousands

explanation.surface: Spend thousands and get a jewel set in a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as a ring' puts GET ONE around MS. Read whole, the clue describes the jewel costing thousands that one gets set as a ring.
explanation.definitionFit: A precious jewel costing thousands is set to make a ring.

clue.text: Given teeth that go wrong — fed up about it

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for sated surrounds the word for err

parts.note: fed up in the sense of full, satiated
to err is to go wrong

explanation.surface: A complaint about things going wrong, from someone who is fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fed up' looks like 'bored' but means full, and 'it' in 'about it' points back to the going wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw-edged blade has a row of notches, so it has been given teeth.

parts.note: to run goods is to carry them secretly, here escaping the customs tax rather than shirking work

explanation.walkthrough: 'Run away' suggests a deserter; 'run' is the smugglers' term for carrying contraband, and 'duty' is customs tax.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving contraband secretly to avoid customs charges is the smuggler's trade.

clue.text: The infernal part of finding key to puzzle

parts.note: E is a musical key
a rebus is a picture puzzle

explanation.surface: Searching for the key to a puzzle is hellish.
explanation.walkthrough: E is a key in music. In Greek myth Erebus is the dark region of the underworld.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this was the darkness through which souls passed into Hades, an underworld region.

parts.note: the spring flowers named after the youth in myth who fell in love with his own reflection, read as belonging to the vain

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloomers' are flowers, not underwear; the flowers are named after the myth of a youth in love with his reflection.
explanation.definitionFit: These daffodil-like flowers take their name from the self-adoring youth of Greek myth.

parts.note: VI is six in Roman numerals, with the possessive S
to age is to mature

explanation.surface: A six-year-old has a grown-up face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mug' is slang for a face, not a cup.
explanation.definitionFit: Mug is slang for the face, and the answer is a literary word for the face.

indicators.note: coming from as in made out of, so the letters of Cape Horn are reworked

explanation.surface: A travelling companion has just sailed in from Cape Horn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming from' rearranges the letters of CAPE HORN.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaperon is an older person who accompanies a young woman, a companion for propriety's sake.

clue.text: Eases the position, in part retreating

indicators.note: in means the word for position goes inside the reversed word
retreating means going backwards, so the word for part is read in reverse

parts.note: to part is to sever
the lie of something is its position, as in the lie of the land

explanation.surface: Troops easing a position by partly falling back.
explanation.walkthrough: The military surface makes 'position' look like a post held by troops and 'part' look like 'partly'; 'part' is the verb, to cut apart.
explanation.definitionFit: To relieve pain or a burden is to lessen it, to make it easier.

clue.text: Cherry wore white for this festival (Housman)

definitions.text: Cherry wore white for this festival (Housman)

parts.words: Cherry wore white for this festival (Housman)
parts.note: Housman's poem Loveliest of Trees has the cherry wearing white blossom for a spring Christian festival

explanation.walkthrough: A. E. Housman's poem 'Loveliest of trees, the cherry now' says the cherry stands 'wearing white for Eastertide'.
explanation.definitionFit: The spring feast celebrating the Resurrection is the tide named in Housman's line about cherry blossom.
